new_statements.quote: According to [5], stress (accent d'intensité) always falls on the first syllable of a word, pëkö ["pEk2] (none, there is nothing), fifikë ["fifikE] (toy). In word derivation, when words obtain a prefix, the stress pattern remains and stress shifts to the inserted first syllable e.g.: malan ["malan] (to fall) vs. amalan ["amalan] (CAUS-fall). Compound words behave in the same way meaning that stress always shifts to the first syllable of the word. Finally, [6] proposes secondary stress in polysyllabic words, with it always falling on the third syllable ["amalan (CAUS-fall)].

new_statements.rule_in_words: As reported secondhand: intensity stress falls on the first syllable of every word, including after prefixation and compounding (stress moves to the new first syllable); stress is demarcative and not weight-sensitive. Secondary stress on the third syllable is Tryon's (1968) addition, not Lenormand's.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not attributed to Lenormand; Torres et al. attribute the third-syllable secondary stress to Tryon 1968 Dehu Grammar.
new_statements.exceptions: None reported in the secondary summary. Lenormand p. 91 (read directly) notes only that the Wet and Lösi dialects differ in sibilants (s/s, z/z) and a few lexical items, and that the vowel system rests on a long/short distinction with glottal closure after short vowels.
new_statements.identity_note: Lenormand 1954 p. 91 (read directly) states that all Lifou speakers share one language, with minor phonological and lexical differences between the Wet (north) and Lösi districts (Wet keeps two extra sibilant phonemes); no dialect-specific stress claim was seen. Torres et al. recorded four female Drehu-French bilingual speakers on Lifou (2018 p. 141); Torres and Fletcher 2020 note possible phonetic change since the 1950s-80s descriptions (retroflex stops now affricates) and a now fully bilingual community.

new_statements.quote: [p. 107] E. Accent d'intensité — L'accent d'intensité, lorsqu'il existe, n'a pas de valeur différenciative, mais, par contre, il a un rôle démarcatif du fait qu'il se trouve toujours sur la première syllabe du mot. Dans les dissyllabes, les trisyllabes et les polysyllabes l'accent est donc placé sur la première syllabe : nuthan, pëkô, nyima, fifikë, nyacama. [p. 108] Lorsqu'on a à faire à un mot dérivé, l'accent est placé, non sur la première syllabe du radical, mais sur la première syllabe du préfixe [...] Dans les mots composés, l'accent est également placé sur la première syllabe du mot, lorsque celui-ci est senti comme formant un véritable mot unique.
new_statements.translation: E. Stress accent — The stress accent, when it exists, has no distinctive value but does have a demarcative role, since it always falls on the first syllable of the word. In disyllables, trisyllables and polysyllables the accent is therefore placed on the first syllable: nuthan, pëkô, nyima, fifikë, nyacama. With a derived word the accent is placed not on the first syllable of the root but on the first syllable of the prefix [...] In compound words the accent is likewise placed on the first syllable of the word, when the latter is felt to form a genuine single word.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (accent d'intensite) is non-contrastive and purely demarcative: it always falls on the first syllable of the word, whatever its length (2, 3 or more syllables); in prefixed derivatives the stress moves to the prefix-initial syllable (amalan < mala), and true compounds likewise carry a single initial stress, which distinguishes a compound from a phrase. Lenormand hedges with 'lorsqu'il existe' (when it exists), and p. 108 repeats that initial stress is the principal word-boundary signal.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing: Lenormand does not mention secondary stress (the catalog's third-syllable secondary comes from Tryon 1968 PL B-7 §1.1, held in our earlier reading).
new_statements.exceptions: None as exceptions; only the qualifications that stress 'lorsqu'il existe' has no distinctive value, that a prefix counts as part of the word (stress on the prefix), and that a compound takes initial stress only 'lorsque celui-ci est senti comme formant un veritable mot unique' (otherwise it is a locution with word-by-word stress).
new_statements.identity_note: Lenormand 1954 describes 'le lifou' (qene dehu / qene Wet) of Lifou island as one language, noting that the Wet (north) and Losi dialects differ only in two sibilant contrasts and a few lexical items; his stress statement is for the language as a whole. Moyse-Faurie 1983 (unread) treats Drehu of Lifou. The catalog record 'Dehu' and the Torres & Fletcher papers ('Drehu') refer to the same language.

readall_conflicts: The descriptive sources (Lenormand 1954, Tryon 1968, as reported by Torres et al.) give fixed initial word stress with a third-syllable secondary, which is what the catalog records. The two instrumental studies already held by the project from the 2026-09-16 pass contradict this at the level of type: Torres, Fletcher and Wigglesworth 2018 (SST, p. 143) found "the vowel of the final syllable is significantly longer than the first vowel.. These duration results do not provide evidence of word initial stress" and that "the lack of any durational or tonal cues associated with word-initial syllables calls for a further investigation, and a revaluation of previous stress analyses of Drehu"; Torres and Fletcher 2020 (JASA 147(4), p. 2955) conclude "Contrary to earlier impressionistic accounts (Lenormand, 1954; Tryon, 1968a), this study on tonal alignment supports the claim that a phrasal rather than strictly lexical prominence marking is found in Drehu", describing an initial L tone and a prominence-lending H at the right edge of the prosodic word, while adding that right-edge prominence "could also be associated with word final delimitative stress but also this hypothesis requires further investigation". So the alternative reading to the catalog's fixed: initial syllable is phrase-level prominence only (or possibly right-edge/final demarcative stress); the 2018 study measured words only under informational focus, and the 2020 study examined short NPs, so neither settles the word-l…

sources.quote: 'Previous descriptions of Drehu phonology claimed that the language has initial word stress. ... Contrary to our predictions, it was found that vowel duration was significantly longer on the final syllable of target tokens. Similarly, a rise was often observed, which in 97.6% of the cases ended on a peak at the right edge of the constituent. ... the lack of any durational or tonal cues associated with word-initial syllables calls for a further investigation, and a revaluation of previous stress analyses of Drehu' (4 female speakers, words in informational focus).
sources.note: First acoustic test of the initial-stress claim (no durational/tonal cue on initial syllables; final-syllable lengthening and right-edge F0 peak); now obtained by the project.
